issues.legal_issue: Inherent procedural powers cannot be used, after prolonged inaction, to reopen a settled land record without a sufficient explanation, particularly where affected persons were not notified and no fraud or collusion was alleged.
material_facts: A land record finally published in 1957 treated the land as retainable by the intermediary.
The State took no steps to correct the record for nearly 38 years, during which the land changed hands and the current owners obtained approvals and began construction.

In 1995, after the State had lost earlier litigation concerning the construction, an officer used inherent civil-court powers to reopen the record, describing it as anomalous and defective but alleging no fraud or misrepresentation.

Notice was directed to a company that had gone into liquidation rather than the current owners, and there was no evidence that the owners were served with notice of the proceeding or its resulting order.
The State gave no satisfactory explanation for its inaction and did not use the specific statutory process for revising the record.
issues.conclusion: The reopening order was invalid, and the High Court was right to set it aside; the State could not use inherent powers to reopen the settled matter in the manner attempted.
issues.legal_principle: Section 57A of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953 empowers the State Government to invest specified authorities with civil-court powers, but those powers under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be used to reopen settled matters, especially where specific statutory provisions address the situation. Their use after prolonged unexplained delay, without notice to affected persons and without any allegation of fraud or collusion, would be an abuse of power.

rule.if: appeal_against_reopening_order and finally_published_record and prolonged_unexplained_delay and inherent_power_used_to_reopen and (affected_persons_not_notified or no_fraud_or_collusion_alleged)

predicates.appeal_against_reopening_order: The proceeding is an appeal concerning an order that reopened a previously finalized land record.
predicates.finally_published_record: A land record had been formally completed and finally published before the later reopening attempt.
predicates.prolonged_unexplained_delay: The authority took no corrective action for a prolonged period and gave no satisfactory explanation for the delay.
predicates.inherent_power_used_to_reopen: The authority relied on inherent procedural powers to reopen the finalized record.
predicates.affected_persons_not_notified: The authority did not notify the persons whose interests in the land were affected by the reopening.
predicates.no_fraud_or_collusion_alleged: The authority did not allege fraud or collusion in the preparation of the finalized record.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns reopening a finally published land record through inherent powers after prolonged unexplained inaction, and the affected persons were not notified or no fraud or collusion was alleged, the reopening order is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: An intermediary may retain land comprised in or appertaining to buildings or structures it owns even when the premises are tenanted, and khas possession is not required for retention under that provision.
material_facts: The intermediary granted a composite lease covering land together with buildings and structures on it; the lease commenced before the date of vesting.
The final land record treated the land as retainable under the provision concerning land comprised in or appertaining to buildings and structures owned by an intermediary.
The premises were occupied by a tenant when the Act came into force, but the relevant retention provision did not require khas possession.
There was no finding or evidence that a mill stood on the land on the date of vesting.
issues.conclusion: The land was retainable under Section 6(1)(b); tenancy did not prevent retention, and the provisions concerning land comprised in a mill did not apply on the facts.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6(1)(b) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953 does not require khas possession and permits retention of land comprised in or appertaining to buildings or structures owned by the intermediary, including where those premises are tenanted under a composite lease. Section 6(1)(g), the proviso to Section 6(2), and Section 6(3) did not apply because no mill was shown to have stood on the land on the date of vesting. State of West Bengal v. Scene Screen (Pvt.) Ltd. (2000) 7 SCC 686 held that Section 6(1)(b) does not require khas possession; Saroj Kumar Bose v. Kanallal Mondal (1985) 3 SCC 717 likewise recognized that khas possession is required only where the Act expressly says so. State of West Bengal v. Suburban Agriculture Dairy & Fisheries Pvt. Ltd. (1993 Supp. (4) SCC 674) concerned tank fisheries and different provisions, so it did not govern this composite lease of buildings, structures, and land.

rule.if: land_retention_proceeding and intermediary_owned_buildings_or_structures and land_appurtenant_to_those_buildings and premises_were_tenanted and no_mill_on_land_at_vesting

predicates.land_retention_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether an intermediary may retain land after statutory vesting.
predicates.intermediary_owned_buildings_or_structur: The intermediary owned buildings or structures situated on the land.
predicates.land_appurtenant_to_those_buildings: The land was comprised in or appertained to the intermediary's buildings or structures.
predicates.premises_were_tenanted: A tenant occupied the premises under a lease when vesting occurred.
predicates.no_mill_on_land_at_vesting: No mill was shown to have stood on the land when vesting occurred.

issues.definition: In a land-retention proceeding, an intermediary may retain appurtenant land where it owned the buildings or structures, even if the premises were tenanted, when no mill stood on the land at vesting.

issues.legal_issue: A land-ceiling proceeding is not inapplicable on the ground that land was held by the State when the land had not vested in the State and remained retainable by the intermediary.
material_facts: The State asserted that the land had vested in it and that the land-ceiling law therefore did not apply to the land.
The land was retainable by the intermediary under the provision concerning land comprised in or appertaining to owned buildings and structures, so it had not vested in the State.

A competent authority had issued a land-ceiling statement, and the State had previously challenged its genuineness rather than asserting that the proceedings were outside the law's scope because the land belonged to the State.
The earlier challenge to the genuineness of the statement was rejected, and the State first argued in the appeal that the land-ceiling proceedings were without jurisdiction because of vesting.
issues.conclusion: Because the land had not vested in the State, the State-land exclusion in Section 19 of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 did not apply; the State could not disregard the land-ceiling proceedings on the newly raised jurisdictional ground.
issues.legal_principle: Section 19 of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 excludes specified land held by a State Government from the application of Chapter II. Since the land was retainable by the intermediary and did not vest in the State under Sections 4 and 5 of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, the State-land exclusion did not apply. The State's belated jurisdictional argument was inconsistent with its earlier position and was not the basis on which it had initiated the reopening proceedings.

rule.if: challenge_to_land_ceiling_proceeding and land_did_not_vest_in_state and land_remained_retainable_by_intermediary and prior_genuineness_challenge_rejected

predicates.challenge_to_land_ceiling_proceeding: The proceeding includes a challenge to the applicability or effect of a land-ceiling determination.
predicates.land_did_not_vest_in_state: The land did not become the State's property through statutory vesting.
predicates.land_remained_retainable_by_intermediary: The intermediary remained entitled to retain the land under the applicable retention rule.
predicates.prior_genuineness_challenge_rejected: An earlier challenge alleging that the land-ceiling determination was not genuine had been rejected.

issues.definition: Where a land-ceiling determination is challenged, the land did not vest in the State, the intermediary remained entitled to retain it, and an earlier challenge to the determination's genuineness was rejected, the State cannot disregard the determination as inapplicable.
